title: In 186 mouse brain regions, neuronal Kv3 transcripts predicted shorter spikes beyond space and random genes, but T-type calcium transcripts did not predict bursts (IBL, Allen atlas)
abstract: Question: earlier work found that the neuron-type mix of a mouse brain region predicts its intrinsic spiking phenotype better than input wiring, but not which property of the type mix acts. We tested whether ion-channel transcripts predict the matching spike feature. Data: 62,545 IBL Brain-Wide Map units in 186 regions; the expected log expression of 20,378 genes per region, from Allen MERFISH type composition multiplied by 10x type means. The plan was frozen before any gene-to-feature statistic. Results: the Kv3 score (Kcnc1-3) had Spearman rho -0.60 with spike duration (spatial-surrogate p = 0.001; expression-matched random-gene p = 0.004; within divisions -0.28). It stayed after control of technical features, geometry, division and rate (partial -0.25) and in a second MERFISH brain (-0.54). But the Pvalb gene predicted equally well, Kv3 genes ranked only in the top 3% genome-wide, and the Kv3 link to the narrow-unit fraction did not survive controls. The T-type score (Cacna1g/h/i) did not predict burst firing (rho -0.18, against a positive prediction). In 27 thalamic nuclei it correlated negatively with burst fraction (-0.53), and cortical input share kept its link after control of the T-type genes (partial 0.71). In held-out spatial blocks, transcriptome PCs predicted intrinsic features better than input-wiring PCs (mean CV R2 0.39 vs 0.30; 7 of 8 features). Ion-channel genes beat random gene sets modestly (p = 0.036). Limitations: correlational region averages; expected transcripts, not channel protein; the IBL drift control is rate-linked.
